title: TCP and UDP: two ways to send
summary: TCP opens a connection and makes sure everything arrives in order; UDP just sends. Knowing which one a service uses tells you how to test it.

scheme: in order, or you get an error
one may be lost, late, out of order
text: Both carry data between two ports. They don't promise the same thing.
- TCP resends what's lost: web pages, SSH, databases, mail.
- UDP is lighter and faster to start: DNS queries, video calls, games, time sync. The program copes with losses itself, or asks again.
- HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which is built on UDP.

scheme: DNS on UDP 53, SSH on TCP 22
text: A port number belongs to one protocol: TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are two different doors.
- ss -tuln lists what listens: t TCP, u UDP, l listening, n numbers (Linux; on a Mac: lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN).
- A firewall rule opens a port for TCP or for UDP: open the wrong one and the service stays unreachable.
- DNS mostly uses UDP 53, and TCP 53 for big answers: open both.

scheme: TCP port, nothing listening  → refused, at once
TCP port, firewall drops     → time out
test a UDP service with a real question:
text: TCP answers clearly: connected, refused or nothing. UDP has no connection, so silence proves little.
- A closed UDP port may send back an ICMP error, or nothing at all if a firewall drops it.
- So test a UDP service by asking it a real question it should answer: a DNS query to that server.
